--- title: "The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back" description: "Emigration from Greece since the debt crisis, in Eurostat data: how many left, who they were, where they went, who came back, and whether it was a brain drain." author: "" date: "27 November 2026" --- ## What is this? From 2010 until August 2018, Greece lived on rescue loans, through three programmes ([ESM](https://www.esm.europa.eu/assistance/greece/greece-successfully-concludes-esm-programme)). In those years many people left the country. This story asks five questions about them: 1. **How many people left Greece, and when?** 2. **Who left?** Their age and sex, and whether they were Greek citizens or foreigners. 3. **Where did they go?** 4. **Did they come back?** 5. **Was it a brain drain?** Did those who left have more education than those who stayed? [Fewer and Older](ILLUSTRATION_GREEK_POPULATION.Rmd) shows how births, deaths and migration change the size and the age of Greece's population. This story follows the people who left. The data come from **Eurostat**, the statistical office of the EU, and are downloaded when the page is rendered: - **Greece's figures** on the people who leave the country and those who arrive, each year, from ELSTAT, the Hellenic Statistical Authority: by age and sex (migr_emi2), by citizenship (migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz), by country of birth (migr_imm3ctb) and by where they went (migr_emi5nxt); with the population (demo_pjan) and unemployment (une_rt_a). - **The figures of the countries they moved to**: the Greek citizens who arrive in each European country and those who leave it (migr_imm1ctz, migr_emi1ctz), and those who live there (migr_pop1ctz). - **The Labour Force Survey**, a survey of households in the countries of the EU and EFTA, which asks people where they were born and what education they have (lfst_lmbpcobed, edat_lfs_9912). **Most of these figures are estimates.** In the statistics of the EU, an emigrant is someone who moves abroad for at least 12 months ([Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_immi_esms.htm)). Greece does not count them: nobody has to tell the authorities that they are leaving, so ELSTAT calls its data on emigration "essentially non-existent" and estimates it instead. For 2011 to 2021, emigration is the number of people who must have left for the population, as revised after the census of 2021, to add up with the births, the deaths and the people who arrived. Since 2022, it is worked out from the number of people that Germany counts arriving from Greece ([ELSTAT](https://www.statistics.gr/en/statistics/-/publication/SPO15/-)). The countries the emigrants go to count the people who arrive, but not all in the same way: Norway, for example, counts as migrants the people who move for six months ([Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_immi_esms.htm)). --- ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite")) library(eurostat) library(plotly) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) { x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="num",cache=FALSE) x<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),]) result<-x[order(x$time),] return(result) } # the years that Eurostat flags as a break in one series (flag b); the eurostat package leaves the # flags out when it filters, so they come from Eurostat's own API, in JSON-stat breaks_in<-function(id,filters) { api<-"https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/" query<-paste(paste0(names(filters),"=",unlist(filters)),collapse="&") x<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(api,id,"?",query)) years<-names(sort(unlist(x$dimension$time$category$index))) flags<-unlist(x$status) result<-as.numeric(years[as.integer(names(flags)[flags=="b"])+1]) return(result) } # all ages, both sexes, age in completed years, numbers of people everyone<-list(age="TOTAL",sex="T",agedef="COMPLET",unit="NR") # Greece: the people who left each year, by sex and single year of age, and the breaks in the series emigration<-eurostat_values("migr_emi2",list(geo="EL",agedef="COMPLET",unit="NR")) breaks<-breaks_in("migr_emi2",c(list(geo="EL"),everyone)) # Greece: everyone (TOTAL) and the Greek citizens (NAT) among the people who left and among those # who arrived; the people who arrived who were born in Greece (NAT); and the people who left, by # group of country of next residence: another EU country, or a country outside the EU left<-eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz",c(list(geo="EL",citizen=c("NAT","TOTAL")),everyone)) came<-eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz",c(list(geo="EL",citizen=c("NAT","TOTAL")),everyone)) came_born<-eurostat_values("migr_imm3ctb",c(list(geo="EL",c_birth="NAT"),everyone)) next_residence<-eurostat_values("migr_emi5nxt",list(geo="EL",unit="NR")) # every country that reports them, but not Greece itself or the EU as a whole: the Greek citizens # (EL) who arrived there each year, those who left, and those who lived there on 1 January abroad<-function(x) { result<-x[!x$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020"),] return(result) } greeks_came<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz",c(list(citizen="EL"),everyone))) greeks_left<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz",c(list(citizen="EL"),everyone))) greeks_living<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_pop1ctz", list(citizen="EL",age="TOTAL",sex="T",unit="NR"))) # Greece: the population on 1 January, by sex and single year of age, and unemployment, % of the # labour force aged 15 to 74 population<-eurostat_values("demo_pjan",list(geo="EL",sex=c("T","M","F"),unit="NR")) unemployment<-eurostat_values("une_rt_a",list(geo="EL",age="Y15-74",sex="T",unit="PC_ACT")) # Labour Force Survey: the people born in Greece who live in another EU or EFTA country, by age # group and education, thousands; and those who live in Greece, aged 15 to 64, by education, % born_abroad<-eurostat_values("lfst_lmbpcobed",list(c_birth="EL",c_resid="EU27_2020_EFTA")) born_home<-eurostat_values("edat_lfs_9912",list(geo="EL",c_birth="NAT",sex="T",age="Y15-64")) # the names of the countries of the EU and EFTA, and of the United Kingdom country_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code), setNames(efta_countries$name,efta_countries$code),UK="United Kingdom") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # one series of a dataset, in the order of the years by_year<-function(x,years) { result<-x$values[match(years,x$time)] return(result) } # Greece, year by year: the people who left, all of them and the Greek citizens; the people who # arrived, all of them, the Greek citizens and those born in Greece; and the population total_left<-emigration[emigration$age=="TOTAL"&emigration$sex=="T",] flows<-data.frame(year=total_left$time,left=total_left$values) flows$left_greek<-by_year(left[left$citizen=="NAT",],flows$year) flows$came<-by_year(came[came$citizen=="TOTAL",],flows$year) flows$came_greek<-by_year(came[came$citizen=="NAT",],flows$year) flows$came_born<-by_year(came_born,flows$year) flows$net_greek<-flows$came_greek-flows$left_greek everyone_living<-population[population$age=="TOTAL"&population$sex=="T",] flows$population<-by_year(everyone_living,flows$year) latest<-max(flows$year) flow<-function(column,year) { result<-flows[[column]][match(year,flows$year)] return(result) } # the years of the rescue loans: the first programme started in 2010, and the third and last ended # in August 2018 (ESM) rescue<-c(2010,2018) rescue_years<-rescue[1]:rescue[2] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} greek_red<-"#d62728" blue<-"#1f77b4" orange<-"#ff7f0e" gray<-"#9e9e9e" light_gray<-"#ebebeb" dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the color of the notes # the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(), margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) { note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left", yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray)) result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"), yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis), margin=margin,annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>% config(displaylogo=FALSE) return(result) } legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom") # the years of the rescue loans, shaded behind the data rescue_band<-list(type="rect",xref="x",yref="paper",x0=rescue[1]-0.5,x1=rescue[2]+0.5,y0=0,y1=1, fillcolor=light_gray,line=list(width=0),layer="below") shaded<-paste0("Shaded: the rescue loans, ",rescue[1],"–",rescue[2],".") # numbers in the text number<-function(x) { result<-format(x,big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE) return(result) } thousands<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,-3),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE) return(result) } percent<-function(x,digits=0) { result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits),"%") return(result) } one<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1) return(result) } and_list<-function(x) { if(length(x)<2) { return(paste(x)) } result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1)) return(result) } # years as ranges: 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019 give "2014–2016, 2019" years_text<-function(years) { years<-sort(unique(years)) starts<-years[c(TRUE,diff(years)>1)] ends<-years[c(diff(years)>1,TRUE)] result<-paste(ifelse(starts==ends,starts,paste0(starts,"–",ends)),collapse=", ") return(result) } ``` ::: --- ## 1. How many people left Greece, and when? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} in_2000s<-flows$left[flows$year%in%2000:2009] peak_year<-flows$year[which.max(flows$left)] per_1000<-function(year) { result<-1000*flow("left",year)/flow("population",year) return(result) } left_rescue<-sum(flows$left[flows$year%in%rescue_years]) left_greek_rescue<-sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year%in%rescue_years]) over_100k<-flows$year[flows$left>1e5] # the last year in which more people left than the year before: the fall since goes on to the # latest year rose<-flows$year[c(FALSE,diff(flows$left)>=0)] falling_since<-max(rose) jobless<-function(year) { result<-unemployment$values[unemployment$time==year] return(result) } jobless_peak<-unemployment$time[which.max(unemployment$values)] jobless_latest<-max(unemployment$time) ``` ::: **About 41,000 a year in the 2000s; more than 100,000 a year in 2011–2019.** From 2000 to 2009, between 37,433 and 46,993 people left Greece each year. Then came the crisis: 62,041 left in 2010, 106,398 in 2011 and 135,073 in 2012, the most since the figures start in 1991: 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece. In the years of the rescue loans, from 2010 to 2018, 1,018,000 people left, 527,000 of them Greek citizens. The number has fallen every year since 2018, to 78,014 in 2024, 1.9 times the average of the 2000s. It rose with unemployment, which went from 9.8% of the labour force in 2009 to 27.8% in 2013; both have fallen since, unemployment to 8.9% in 2025 (Eurostat, une_rt_a). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bars<-flows[!is.na(flows$left),] rescue_label<-list(x=mean(rescue),y=1,xref="x",yref="paper",yanchor="bottom", text=paste0("Rescue loans, ",rescue[1],"–",rescue[2]),showarrow=FALSE, font=list(size=12,color=dark_gray)) plot_ly(bars,x=~year,y=~left/1000,type="bar",name="People who left", marker=list(color=greek_red, pattern=list(shape=ifelse(bars$year%in%breaks,"/",""),fillmode="overlay", fgcolor="white")), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand") %>% chart("People who left Greece each year, thousands", "Eurostat, migr_emi2 (estimates of ELSTAT). Striped: a break in the series.","Thousands", annotations=list(rescue_label),shapes=list(rescue_band),showlegend=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Eurostat marks a break in the series in 2002, 2008 and 2010 (the striped bars): the method changed, so the years before and after a break cannot be compared closely. --- ## 2. Who left? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the age of a Eurostat age code: Y_LT1 is under one, Y_OPEN and Y_GE100 are the oldest, and the # codes of totals, such as TOTAL, give NA age_of<-function(code) { age<-suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^Y","",code))) age[code=="Y_LT1"]<-0 age[code%in%c("Y_OPEN","Y_GE100")]<-100 result<-age return(result) } group_names<-c("0–14","15–19","20–24","25–29","30–34","35–39","40–44","45–49","50–54","55–59", "60–64","65+") age_group<-function(code) { result<-cut(age_of(code),c(-1,14,19,24,29,34,39,44,49,54,59,64,Inf),labels=group_names) return(result) } # the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age group who lived in Greece on # 1 January rates<-function(year,sex) { out<-emigration[emigration$time==year&emigration$sex==sex,] living<-population[population$time==year&population$sex==sex,] result<-1000*tapply(out$values,age_group(out$age),sum)/ tapply(living$values,age_group(living$age),sum) return(result) } rate<-function(year,sex,group) { result<-rates(year,sex)[[group]] return(result) } # the age that half of the people are younger than or as old as median_age<-function(x) { x<-x[!is.na(age_of(x$age)),] x<-x[order(age_of(x$age)),] result<-age_of(x$age)[which(cumsum(x$values)>=sum(x$values)/2)[1]] return(result) } men_left<-emigration[emigration$age=="TOTAL"&emigration$sex=="M",] men_share<-data.frame(year=men_left$time, share=round(100*men_left$values/flow("left",men_left$time),1)) # the longest run of years in which the share of men is the same runs<-rle(men_share$share) run_end<-cumsum(runs$lengths)[which.max(runs$lengths)] same_years<-men_share$year[(run_end-max(runs$lengths)+1):run_end] middle_aged<-c("35–39","40–44","45–49","50–54") men_to_women<-rates(peak_year,"M")[middle_aged]/rates(peak_year,"F")[middle_aged] ``` ::: **Mostly people in their twenties and thirties, and in the worst years, mostly men.** In 2012, 65% of the people who left Greece were men. Half of them were 32 or younger, while half of the people who lived in Greece were 41 or older. The chart counts the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age who lived in Greece at the start of the year. In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left, and 28 of every 1,000 women. From 35 to 54, men left at 2.3 to 3.5 times the rate of women. In 2024, fewer left: 31 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29, and 34 of every 1,000 women. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} profile<-data.frame(group=factor(group_names,levels=group_names)) lines<-data.frame(year=c(peak_year,peak_year,latest,latest), sex=c("M","F","M","F"), name=paste(c("Men,","Women,","Men,","Women,"), c(peak_year,peak_year,latest,latest)), color=c(blue,orange,blue,orange), dash=c("solid","solid","dot","dot")) p<-plot_ly(profile,x=~group) for(k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) { p<-add_trace(p,y=as.numeric(rates(lines$year[k],lines$sex[k])),type="scatter", mode="lines+markers",name=lines$name[k], line=list(color=lines$color[k],width=3,dash=lines$dash[k]), marker=list(color=lines$color[k]), hovertemplate=paste0("Aged %{x}: %{y:.1f} per 1,000",lines$name[k], "")) } p %>% chart("People who left Greece, per 1,000 of their sex and age", "Eurostat, migr_emi2 and demo_pjan (estimates of ELSTAT).","Per 1,000", y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: These shares are estimates too. ELSTAT does not measure the age and sex of the people who leave: it spreads its estimate of the total with fixed proportions ([ELSTAT](https://www.statistics.gr/en/statistics/-/publication/SPO15/-)). In every year from 2016 to 2020, for example, 56.7% of those who left were men. So the chart shows the broad picture, not the changes from one year to the next. ### Greek citizens and foreigners ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} citizens<-flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek),] citizens$left_foreign<-citizens$left-citizens$left_greek greek_share<-function(year) { result<-100*flow("left_greek",year)/flow("left",year) return(result) } mostly_greek<-citizens$year[citizens$left_greek>citizens$left_foreign] most_greek<-citizens$year[which.max(citizens$left_greek/citizens$left)] foreign<-function(year) { result<-citizens$left_foreign[citizens$year==year] return(result) } ``` ::: In 2008, 44% of the people who left Greece were Greek citizens; the rest were foreigners who had lived in Greece. In 2011–2017, most of those who left were Greek citizens: 58% in 2011, and 70,696 people in 2012. Foreigners left in larger numbers too, 64,377 in 2012 against 23,956 in 2008. In 2024, 32,141 Greek citizens left, 41% of all who left. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(citizens,x=~year,y=~left_greek/1000,type="bar",name="Greek citizens", marker=list(color=greek_red), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandGreek citizens") %>% add_trace(y=~left_foreign/1000,name="Foreign citizens",marker=list(color=gray), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandForeign citizens") %>% chart("People who left Greece, by citizenship, thousands", paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (estimates of ELSTAT).",shaded),"Thousands", shapes=list(rescue_band),barmode="stack",legend=legend_top) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 3. Where did they go? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} next_year<-max(next_residence$time) went<-function(partner) { result<-next_residence$values[next_residence$partner==partner&next_residence$time==next_year] return(result) } to_eu<-went("EU27_2020_FOR") outside<-went("NEU27_2020_FOR") # the years with figures for Germany, the main destination, after the gap of the crisis years since<-min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo=="DE"&greeks_came$time>2008]) window<-since:latest counted<-greeks_came[greeks_came$time%in%window,] destinations<-aggregate(values~geo,counted,sum) destinations<-destinations[order(-destinations$values),] left_window<-sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year%in%window]) counted_total<-sum(destinations$values) not_counted<-left_window-counted_total shown<-head(destinations,10) other<-counted_total-sum(shown$values) # a country's name, with the years it has figures for when they are not all the years label<-function(geo) { name<-if(geo%in%names(country_name)) country_name[[geo]] else geo years<-counted$time[counted$geo==geo] if(length(years)==length(window)) name else paste0(name," (",years_text(years),")") } shown$label<-sapply(shown$geo,label) share_of_counted<-function(geo) { result<-100*shown$values[shown$geo==geo]/counted_total return(result) } # the countries of the EU and EFTA without figures on Greek citizens arriving in these years silent<-setdiff(names(country_name),c(unique(counted$geo),"EL","UK")) uk_years<-counted$time[counted$geo=="UK"] uk_rank<-function(year) { in_year<-counted[counted$time==year,] result<-sum(in_year$values>in_year$values[in_year$geo=="UK"])+1 return(result) } ``` ::: **Above all to Germany. But the countries they went to counted only 55% of them arriving.** Greece's figures say only whether the people who left went to another EU country or outside the EU, not to which country: in 2024, 28,047 went to another EU country and 49,967 outside the EU, foreigners leaving Greece included (migr_emi5nxt). So the chart looks from the other end, at the countries that count the people who arrive, by citizenship. It follows the 545,000 Greek citizens who left Greece from 2014 to 2024, the years with figures for Germany, to the countries that counted them arriving. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # where they went, from top to bottom: not counted, the countries from the most, the others went_to<-data.frame(label=c(paste0("Not counted arriving in Europe: ",thousands(not_counted)), paste0(shown$label,": ",thousands(shown$values)), paste0("Other European countries: ",thousands(other))), value=c(not_counted,shown$values,other), color=c(gray,rep(blue,nrow(shown)+1)), link=c("rgba(158, 158, 158, 0.35)", rep("rgba(31, 119, 180, 0.3)",nrow(shown)+1))) # the place of each node, as a share of the width and of the height (its middle), fixed so that # plotly keeps this order: the nodes share the height of the plot, less a gap of `pad` pixels # between two pad<-10 margin<-list(t=60,b=80,l=10,r=10) # opts_chunk has the dots per inch that set the height of a plotly chart; opts_current has them # multiplied by fig.retina dpi<-knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi") plot_height<-knitr::opts_current$get("fig.height")*dpi-margin$t-margin$b gap<-pad/plot_height node_height<-went_to$value/sum(went_to$value)*(1-gap*(nrow(went_to)-1)) middle<-cumsum(node_height+gap)-gap-node_height/2 plot_ly(type="sankey",orientation="h",arrangement="fixed",valueformat=",.0f", textfont=list(size=12), node=list(label=c(paste0("Left Greece: ",thousands(left_window)),went_to$label), color=c(dark_gray,went_to$color),x=c(0.001,rep(0.999,nrow(went_to))), y=c(0.5,middle),pad=pad,thickness=16,line=list(width=0), hovertemplate="%{label}"), link=list(source=rep(0,nrow(went_to)),target=seq_len(nrow(went_to)), value=went_to$value,color=went_to$link, hovertemplate="%{target.label}")) %>% chart(paste0("Where the Greek citizens who left went, ",since,"–",latest), paste0("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (Greece's estimate) and ", "migr_imm1ctz (the countries' counts). ", "In brackets: the years with figures."),margin=margin,note_y=-0.04) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Germany counted 153,000 Greek citizens arriving, 51% of all those counted in Europe, and the Netherlands 37,000, 12%. The United Kingdom has figures only for 2015, when 12,148 Greek citizens arrived there, the most after Germany; Eurostat's figures for the United Kingdom stop with its withdrawal from the EU ([Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_immi_esms.htm)). The other 247,000, 45% of those who left, were not counted arriving in any European country. They may have gone to countries outside Europe; to European countries that have no figures on Greek citizens arriving, Cyprus, Ireland, Malta, Poland, Portugal and Spain; or to countries in years without figures, such as the United Kingdom after 2015. And part of the gap is the difference between Greece's estimate and the counts of the other countries. The figures cannot tell how much of each. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(c(shown$label,"Other European countries"),number(c(shown$values,other))), col.names=c("Country (years with figures)", paste0("Greek citizens who arrived, ",since,"–",latest)),align="lr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Country (years with figures) | Greek citizens who arrived, 2014–2024| |:------------------------------|-------------------------------------:| |Germany | 153,421| |Netherlands | 36,650| |United Kingdom (2015) | 12,148| |Sweden | 12,123| |Belgium (2014–2019, 2023–2024) | 10,668| |Switzerland (2014–2020) | 10,566| |France | 10,250| |Austria | 9,371| |Norway | 6,176| |Italy | 5,976| |Other European countries | 30,707| ::: ::: ### Where they live now ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} living<-greeks_living[greeks_living$geo%in%names(country_name),] newest<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(living,living$geo),function(x) x[which.max(x$time),])) newest<-head(newest[order(-newest$values),],15) living_year<-max(newest$time) newest$label<-ifelse(newest$time==living_year,country_name[newest$geo], paste0(country_name[newest$geo]," (",newest$time,")")) newest<-newest[order(newest$values),] newest$label<-factor(newest$label,levels=newest$label) lived<-function(geo,year) { result<-living$values[living$geo==geo&living$time==year] return(result) } uk_last<-max(living$time[living$geo=="UK"]) uk_place<-sum(living$values[living$time==uk_last]>lived("UK",uk_last))+1 ``` ::: The countries also count the people who live there, by citizenship. Germany had by far the most Greek citizens: 298,398 on 1 January 2025. Its Greek community was as large before the crisis, 297,668 in 2010: the number of people living in a country does not grow by all who arrive, as people also leave, die, or take the citizenship of the country. In the Netherlands, the number of Greek citizens grew from 7,781 in 2010 to 32,924 in 2025. The United Kingdom had 74,970 in 2019, its last year in the figures, the most after Germany. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(newest,x=~values,y=~label,type="bar",orientation="h",marker=list(color=blue), text=number(newest$values),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:,.0f}") %>% chart(paste0("Greek citizens living elsewhere in Europe, 1 January ",living_year), "Eurostat, migr_pop1ctz. In brackets: the last year with figures.", x_axis=list(range=c(0,1.2*max(newest$values)),tickformat=","), margin=list(l=150,t=70,b=70,r=30),note_y=-0.08) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 4. Did they come back? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} turn<-min(flows$year[flows$year>rescue[1]&!is.na(flows$net_greek)&flows$net_greek>0]) after_turn<-flows$year[flows$year>=turn] before_turn<-max(flows$year[flows$year0]) lost<--sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year%in%rescue[1]:(turn-1)]) gained<-sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year%in%after_turn]) born_elsewhere<-flow("came_greek",latest)-flow("came_born",latest) germany<-data.frame(year=min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo=="DE"]):latest) germany$came<-by_year(greeks_came[greeks_came$geo=="DE",],germany$year) germany$left<-by_year(greeks_left[greeks_left$geo=="DE",],germany$year) both<-germany[!is.na(germany$came)&!is.na(germany$left),] before<-both[both$yearrescue[1]]) since_restart<-both[both$year>=restart,] peak_in<-since_restart$year[which.max(since_restart$came-since_restart$left)] more_left<-since_restart$year[since_restart$left>since_restart$came] # the years without figures between the last year before the crisis and the restart gap_years<-(max(before$year)+1):(restart-1) in_germany<-function(column,year) { result<-germany[[column]][germany$year==year] return(result) } left_germany_first<-length(more_left)==1&&more_left==latest ``` ::: **Some have. Since 2023, more Greek citizens move to Greece each year than leave it, by ELSTAT's estimates, but they have made up only a small part of what the crisis took.** From 2010 to 2022, 328,000 more Greek citizens left Greece than moved to it. In 2023 and 2024, for the first time since 2009, more moved to Greece than left: 9,160 and 19,852 more. Together, that is 9% of what was lost from 2010 to 2022. Not all the Greek citizens who move to Greece were born there: in 2024, 51,993 Greek citizens moved to Greece, but only 44,336 people born in Greece, of any citizenship, so at least 7,657 of the Greek citizens were born abroad. The people born in Greece who move to Greece are coming back to the country of their birth: 44,336 in 2024, against 27,604 in 2022 and 17,350 in 2008. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} greek_flows<-flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek),] plot_ly(greek_flows,x=~year,y=~left_greek/1000,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers", name="Greek citizens who left Greece",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3), marker=list(color=greek_red), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandGreek citizens who left") %>% add_trace(y=~came_greek/1000,name="Greek citizens who moved to Greece", line=list(color=blue,width=3),marker=list(color=blue), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandGreek citizens who came") %>% add_trace(y=~came_born/1000,name="People born in Greece who moved to Greece", line=list(color=blue,width=2,dash="dot"), marker=list(color=blue,symbol="circle-open"), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandBorn in Greece, came") %>% chart("Leaving Greece and moving to Greece, thousands a year", paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz and migr_imm3ctb (estimates of ELSTAT).", shaded),"Thousands",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),shapes=list(rescue_band), legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=110,b=90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: These figures are ELSTAT's estimates as well. Since 2022, it estimates the people who arrive, apart from those granted protection, such as refugees, with a model: from the number of the year before and the growth of the economy. It splits them by citizenship and country of birth as in the census of 2021 ([ELSTAT](https://www.statistics.gr/en/statistics/-/publication/SPO15/-)). ### A check from Germany Germany counts the Greek citizens who move there and those who leave, and its figures point the same way. Before the crisis, more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there, in every year with figures from 1998 to 2008: in 2008, 16,079 left and 8,266 arrived. There are no figures for 2009–2013. In 2015, 18,970 Greek citizens moved to Germany and 5,796 left it. In 2024, 8,833 moved there and 9,025 left: for the first time since the figures restart in 2014, more left than came. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(germany,x=~year,y=~came/1000,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers", name="Greek citizens who moved to Germany",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3), marker=list(color=greek_red), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandMoved to Germany") %>% add_trace(y=~left/1000,name="Greek citizens who left Germany",line=list(color=blue,width=3), marker=list(color=blue), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousandLeft Germany") %>% chart("Greek citizens arriving in and leaving Germany, thousands", paste0("Eurostat, migr_imm1ctz and migr_emi1ctz (figures of Germany; none for ", years_text(gap_years),"). ",shaded),"Thousands",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"), shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 5. Was it a brain drain? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} education_names<-c("ED5-8"="Higher education","ED3_4"="Upper secondary", "ED0-2"="At most lower secondary") education_colors<-c("ED5-8"=greek_red,"ED3_4"=gray,"ED0-2"=dark_gray) adults_abroad<-born_abroad[born_abroad$age=="Y20-64"&born_abroad$time>=2005,] level<-function(isced,year) { result<-adults_abroad$values[adults_abroad$isced11==isced&adults_abroad$time==year] return(result) } edu_latest<-max(adults_abroad$time) # the share with higher education: abroad, of those whose education is known; in Greece, as Eurostat # publishes it working_age<-born_abroad[born_abroad$age=="Y15-64"&born_abroad$time>=2005,] known<-working_age[working_age$isced11%in%names(education_names),] share<-aggregate(values~time,known,sum) names(share)<-c("year","known") share$abroad<-100*by_year(known[known$isced11=="ED5-8",],share$year)/share$known share$home<-by_year(born_home[born_home$isced11=="ED5-8",],share$year) share<-share[!is.na(share$home),] behind<-share$year[share$abroad<=share$home] ahead_since<-max(behind)+1 first_share<-min(share$year) last_share<-max(share$year) higher<-function(where,year) { result<-share[[where]][share$year==year] return(result) } ``` ::: **Partly. The people born in Greece who live elsewhere in Europe used to have less education than those at home; now they have more, and many more of them have a degree.** No statistic follows the people who left, so none can say exactly how much education they had. The nearest is Eurostat's Labour Force Survey, which counts the people born in Greece, aged 20 to 64, who live in another EU or EFTA country, by the highest level of education they finished. From 2010 to 2024, the number of them with higher education, a university degree or similar, rose from about 40,000 to 113,000: 2.8 times as many. The number with at most lower secondary schooling hardly changed: about 102,000 in 2010 and 98,000 in 2024. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p<-plot_ly() for(k in names(education_names)) { p<-add_trace(p,data=adults_abroad[adults_abroad$isced11==k,],x=~time,y=~values,type="scatter", mode="lines+markers",name=education_names[[k]], line=list(color=education_colors[[k]],width=if(k=="ED5-8") 3 else 2), marker=list(color=education_colors[[k]]), hovertemplate=paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand",education_names[[k]], "")) } p %>% chart("Greek-born aged 20 to 64 in other EU and EFTA countries", paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed (Labour Force Survey), by education.",shaded),"Thousands", y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: So the Greeks abroad have changed. In 2005, 12% of the people born in Greece aged 15 to 64 who lived in another EU or EFTA country had higher education, against 18% of those who lived in Greece. In 2024, it was 36% against 32%, and those abroad have had more education than those at home in every year since 2017. To change the Greeks abroad so much, those who left in the crisis must have had much more education than those who had left before them. That they also had more than those who stayed is likely, but the survey cannot prove it: it counts the people who live abroad, not those who left. The share with higher education rose in Greece too, from 18% to 32%. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(share,x=~year,y=~abroad,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers", name="Living in another EU or EFTA country",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3), marker=list(color=greek_red), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}%Living abroad") %>% add_trace(y=~home,name="Living in Greece",line=list(color=blue,width=3), marker=list(color=blue), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}%Living in Greece") %>% chart("Born in Greece, aged 15 to 64: share with higher education", paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed and edat_lfs_9912 (Labour Force Survey).",shaded), "% of the age group",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero",ticksuffix="%"), shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **What the data cannot tell:** - **Who left when.** The survey counts the people who live abroad, whenever they left, not those who left in a given year. - **Where they studied.** It does not say whether the degree was earned in Greece or abroad. - **All the countries.** It covers the EU and EFTA countries: not the United Kingdom, which is left out of this series, nor the countries outside Europe. - **Exact numbers.** The survey asks a sample of households, so its figures move from year to year more than the people do. - **What it cost.** No statistic here says whether those who left would have found work in Greece, or what their education cost the country. --- ## So, what does it mean? 1. **The crisis drove a wave of emigration.** By ELSTAT's estimates, 1,018,000 people left Greece in the years of the rescue loans, 527,000 of them Greek citizens. In 2012, 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece left. 2. **They were young, and many were men.** In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left. 3. **Germany took the most**: 51% of the Greek citizens counted arriving in Europe from 2014 to 2024. For 45% of those who left, the figures do not say where they went. 4. **The flow has turned, a little.** Since 2023, more Greek citizens come to Greece than leave it, and in 2024 more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there. But 29,012 more Greek citizens in 2023 and 2024 make up only 9% of the 328,000 lost from 2010 to 2022. 5. **It was partly a brain drain.** The people born in Greece with higher education who live elsewhere in the EU and EFTA are 2.8 times as many as in 2010, and those abroad now have more education than those at home. Most of these numbers are estimates: Greece does not count the people who leave, and the countries they go to count them in their own ways. The direction is clear; the exact numbers are not. --- ## Sources - Eurostat, migration: [migr_emi2](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_emi2/default/table?lang=en) (emigration by age and sex), [migr_emi1ctz](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_emi1ctz/default/table?lang=en) (emigration by citizenship), [migr_emi5nxt](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_emi5nxt/default/table?lang=en) (emigration by group of country of next residence), [migr_imm1ctz](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_imm1ctz/default/table?lang=en) (immigration by citizenship), [migr_imm3ctb](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_imm3ctb/default/table?lang=en) (immigration by country of birth), [migr_pop1ctz](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_pop1ctz/default/table?lang=en) (population by citizenship), and the [metadata of the migration statistics](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_immi_esms.htm) (definitions, breaks in the series, countries' methods). -
